text:
At college, Q could make a room feel as if it had been expecting him. He came in late, coat unbuttoned, hair damp from the shower, and people shifted to make room. Someone asked what he thought of the reading. He had already read it.

His name was Quentin, but he became Q during our first semester, when a professor misread the roster and he answered to the wrong initial. He was good at answering. He was good at nearly everything that required appearing untroubled: exams, dinner parties, apologies, even borrowing a bicycle and returning it with the chain oiled. He could enter a professor’s office to ask for an extension and leave with a recommendation, a book, and an invitation to dinner. If he worried, he kept it somewhere no one could see.

We lived in adjoining rooms in an old dormitory whose windows rattled when trucks crossed the bridge. Q would sit on my floor, his back against my bed, and tell me things he had not told anyone else—or so I thought. He had a girlfriend in another city, a father who called only to discuss stocks, and a fear of becoming someone who could sit through dinner without being asked a question. I mistook this inventory for intimacy. It did not occur to me that a person could be candid and still private.

We shared books, cigarettes, and the habit of walking down to the river after midnight. After graduation, we went to a bar, where Q spoke to everyone and I watched him do it. The next morning he drove away in a borrowed car. Years later, at a wedding, we hugged beside the bar and promised to call. We did not.

After that, I heard about him through other people. He had moved to Chicago, made partner at a firm, married the woman from the wedding, and then, according to a later report, not been married to her anymore. I didn’t ask for details. We retained a knowledge of each other that had grown intimate and useless.

Ten years after graduation, I went to the municipal pool on a wet Tuesday because my apartment was too hot and my knees objected to running. The low brick building smelled of chlorine, coffee, and damp wool. Above the lockers, a painted blue whale regarded the entrance with patient disapproval.

I had been swimming half an hour when I saw Q at the far end, talking to a woman beside the lane ropes. He wore a black swim cap and held goggles in one hand. Even across the pool, I recognized the way he stood, one foot ahead of the other, as if ready to make space for someone. The woman looked about forty, with a towel around her shoulders and the alert, exhausted expression of someone who had waited all day to say something.

I got out and sat behind the glass partition. I could have gone over. Instead, I pretended to adjust my goggles and watched their reflection.

Q hadn’t seen me, or gave no sign that he had. His face was older, the lines around his mouth lending him an attentive look. He still had the dark eyebrows that made people think he was listening when he was actually composing a reply. He had once admitted this to me.

The woman said something. Q nodded.

“I know,” he said. “I should have told you sooner.”

“You’ve said that before.”

He turned the goggles over in his hand. At college, he had done the same with pens, cups, and other people’s silverware whenever words weren’t behaving.

“I thought there might still be a way to—”

“There isn’t.”

“I meant a way to make the transition easier.”

“For whom?”

His face changed. He tried to find the answer that would do the least damage. He had always seemed good at difficult conversations. Once, he had persuaded a dean to let a student stay after a disciplinary hearing. At a party, he had taken a crying classmate outside and returned with her breathing steady and her coat buttoned. We believed he could handle anything if he was allowed to be in the room.

“I know this is upsetting,” he said.

“Don’t tell me what I’m feeling.”

“Right. Sorry.”

“You told me the project was mine.”

“I said you were the person I wanted for it.”

“You said it was mine. Then you gave it to Daniel.”

Q glanced toward the shallow end, where two children splashed beneath the lifeguard’s watch.

“Daniel has more experience with the client.”

“He has six months. I’ve been doing this for nine years.”

“I know.”

“You told me to stop taking every assignment that came along. You said I needed to lead something.”

“I still believe that.”

“Do you?”

He opened his mouth, then shut it. The silence seemed to trouble him more than her questions. His shoulders drew inward.

“I let you believe I had more authority than I did,” he said.

“That’s not what happened.”

“No.”

“You had the authority.”

“Some of it.”

“Q.”

The way she said his name made me look away. I watched a man in a red bathing cap cross the wet tile, his steps soft and careful. When I looked back, Q was explaining that he’d tried to get Daniel through the first meeting, then planned to bring her in. He had thought that would be easier than putting her in front of the client and having them— He stopped before saying what he feared they might do.

“Nothing,” he said. “That was wrong.”

She rubbed her forehead. “It’s always this. You make a decision, then put me in the position of having to comfort you about it.”

“I’m not asking you to comfort me.”

“You’re standing there looking like I hit you with a chair.”

“I don’t know what to say.”

“Then say what happened.”

He nodded, miserable. “They wanted Daniel. I let them have him. I thought I could change their minds later. I didn’t. Then I kept waiting to tell you because I didn’t want you to be angry with me.”

“And now?”

“Now I’m telling you.”

“After I had to ask three times.”

“Yes.”

She shook her head. “That isn’t the same thing.”

“No.”

The goggles’ strap had left a red mark across his palm. For once he seemed not to know what his hands were for. It was a small sight, but something in me loosened. Not pleasure. More like the end of an argument I had been having with him alone.

At college, Q’s competence had seemed like a moral quality. I admired him, with a little resentment. I thought that if I could be more like him, I might stop making mistakes other people had to notice. He forgot nothing. He could tell someone the truth and make it feel survivable. I believed this because once, when I needed him, he had done something close enough.

The woman pulled her towel tighter. “I have to get back.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He nodded. “I’m sorry.”

She didn’t answer. She picked up her sandals and walked toward the locker room. Q watched her go but didn’t follow. He looked neither noble nor pathetic, only like someone who had made a choice and waited too long to explain it.

I could have gone over then. I could have said his name and watched recognition cross his face. But the woman hadn’t asked for an audience, and he hadn’t asked for me. I also felt that identifying myself would restore him to his old shape: the brilliant friend, the person who knew what to say, who could put a hand on my shoulder and make a moment seem arranged.

So I stayed where I was.

After a minute, Q put on his goggles and got into the pool. He swam slowly, his stroke careful and stiff. At the far end, he paused with both hands on the wall, then pushed off again. The woman came out of the locker room dressed and left without looking toward the water. Q was still swimming when I went.

At the door, I turned once. He stood in the shallow end with water at his waist, pushing back his wet hair though there was little of it to push. He looked across the pool as if he had misplaced something there.

I thought of calling to him, of how easily I once could interrupt his day. I thought of the years in which we had each become real to ourselves in ways the other could not witness. Then I stepped out into the rain.

For a while, I carried the scene as a secret, though it wasn’t useful to anyone. I hadn’t learned what his job was, what project he’d lost, or why the woman had trusted him. I didn’t know whether they would speak again. I knew only that he had failed at something I’d imagined him good at, and that he had looked like a person trying to get through a day without knowing what he should have done.

It didn’t make him less admirable. It made my admiration less convenient. On the bus home, the windows fogged and the city passed in wet fragments. I remembered the boy in the adjoining dormitory telling me he feared becoming someone no one asked questions of. I’d thought he was being dramatic. Perhaps he had been. Perhaps he had been telling the truth in the only form he knew.

The next morning, I wondered whether he had noticed me behind the glass. He might have recognized my reflection. He might have decided, as I had, not to say anything. I couldn’t tell which possibility I preferred.

A week later, I went back to the pool. Q wasn’t there. I swam six lengths, then stopped at the wall. A woman in the next lane asked if I was finished with the kickboard. I handed it to her.

“Thanks,” she said.

“Of course,” I answered, with the easy confidence of someone asked something simple. Then I watched her carry it away.
